video.titulo: The Earthquake That Has Already Hit the Northwest 5 Times — And It Isn't the Big One
video.descricao:
Sources: https://tinyurl.com/critical21
Emergency Preparedness Guide: https://payhip.com/b/GWENV

The Pacific Northwest has been bracing for the wrong earthquake, and the right one has already hit five times.

Everyone out there knows about the Big One — the magnitude 9 on the Cascadia subduction zone, roughly every five hundred years. That one is real. It is not the one that has actually put brick into the streets of Seattle. Underneath Puget Sound, a slab of ocean floor is tearing itself apart tens of miles down, and the Pacific Northwest Seismic Network describes that kind of earthquake as the most common source of damaging shaking in Washington and Oregon.

The record: 1909, 1939, then April thirteenth 1949, magnitude 7.1, eight dead. April twenty-ninth 1965, magnitude 6.5, seven dead. February twenty-eighth 2001, the Nisqually earthquake, magnitude 6.8 at fifty-two kilometres depth, one death and around two billion dollars in damage in forty seconds. The U.S.G.S. puts an 85 percent chance on another magnitude 6.5 or greater deep earthquake in the region within fifty years.

Seattle has about 1,100 unreinforced masonry buildings on its own public inventory and no law requiring anyone to fix them. Portland has about 1,600, passed a placard ordinance in 2019 requiring owners to post a sign, got sued on First Amendment grounds, lost in federal court, repealed it, and took its public database offline.

And the earthquake in Colombia on August tenth, magnitude 7.4 at 107 kilometres depth, which ran this experiment in public: two cities in the coffee region, forty-five kilometres apart, one rebuilt to a new seismic code after 1999 and one not, and completely different mornings.

CHAPTERS

0:00 The earthquake in Colombia that started this
3:26 Two different earthquakes under the Northwest
5:26 Five times since 1909
8:17 The thirty-year number, and what it does not mean
9:54 The brick buildings in Seattle and Portland

lista.texto: I was a boy in Tacoma in 1965. I was in bed. My bed slid on the wooden floor from wall to wall. The ceiling in the hallway had a 6 foot crack, but that was about it. As for the 2001 Nisqually quake, I was at work in Seattle in a 6 story 90 year old brick hospital.  My office was in the only un-retrofitted part of the original building. It lasted about 35 seconds, during which the elevator wall outside my office collapsed, the ceiling was coming down, and the stairwell was damaged, becoming unusable for months. My boss and I ran down the hall to the new EQ-safe building. Many may know of those metal strips in the floors of large public buildings. Well, those are there so allow different parts to move at different rates and in different directions during an EQ. When we got to the junction of the two buildings, the metal strip had fallen into a void as the buildings were separating and then hitting each other about every 2 seconds.  When the building would separate, we could see all the way to the ground 6 floors below.  We jumped across the 18 inch "chasm" as the EQ was winding down. My home had minor cracks in ceiling plaster. I have since had my home wrapped horizontally and vertically with metal tape, the city made me add steel reinforcement in walls during a big remodel, and had the house bolted to the foundation. I live 2.5 blocks from a depression in the road and waviness in the curbs that probably mark the line of the Seattle Fault. I'm expecting the next every-30-years EQ described here (called a Benioff zone quake) any time before I'm out of my house (hopefully 20+ years). I have solar panels and full home batteries, which can power my electric car,  I grow my own veggies. and I make my own alcohol (wine).  I'm as ready as I can be.
That’s an incredible firsthand comparison. Being inside an older, unretrofitted brick building during Nisqually must have been terrifying. Glad you and your coworkers made it out safely.

I live  in Santa Monica California (Los Angeles County) used to live in San Francisco. My house is new and built to current earthquake codes for California and the office I work in has been retrofitted to current California earthquake codes. I have a storm shelter with a month’s worth of food and supplies in the case of an actual earthquake emergency.  The biggest earthquake I was in: Loma Prieta in San Francisco October 17th 1989. I was at the A’s-Giants World Series game! 15 seconds of pure adrenaline and fear! I’m glad I wasn’t on the Bay Bridge and especially not on the Cypress Expressway!  I do have a friend in Washington State on BainBridge Island near Seattle and I do worry about him as Cascadia can have a Magnitude 9 earthquake!  He’s worried about me being in LA and the San Andreas Fault! Guess we are gluttons for punishment!
Excellent presentation. I live close to the Nisqually, so it hit home to me. Thank you for encouraging use to be prepared.

I will never forget the 2001 Nisqually quake. I was at home, in an apartment on the third floor of a small four story building in North Seattle that was built in 1977. At first, my roommate and I noticed our computer monitors were shaking in an odd way. Within seconds, we realized what was happening. With a cat in one arm and a laptop in the other, I quickly sat down on the floor under the door jam of our front door. My roommate was sitting directly across from me. We could feel the building moving back and forth underneath us in a terrifying way. At one point, I thought the whole building was going to collapse. When the shaking finally ended, we immediately went outside and found lots of other dazed and confused neighbors doing the same thing. My cat grew restless, and the building seemed fine, so we went back in moments later.

Great job on your video! I remember the 1965 earthquake very well. I was just about to step off of the school bus onto the concrete sidewalk when everything began to shake. The sidewalk I was about to step down onto became like a wave. It seemed unreal to see that concrete sidewalk become more like a fluid as the earth shook. Moments later that concrete was just as solid as it had been before the quake and was undamaged.
Thanks for watching! That sounds like one of the wildest ways to experience an earthquake, glad you were ok!

I was observing a middle school class at a school in Seattle when the Nisqually quake hit. After hearing a growing low roar, the walls began shaking and waves began rolling across the floor. Everyone talked about that event for a long time afterward, and I hope that generation of students has taken their respect for earthquakes--and earthquake preparedness--into adulthood. I'd like to think some of those kids are now community leaders or even council members or legislators, ready to take the kind of action you described in the video. Great work!

My Dad had built quake secure shelving for all my mom's books after the Scotts Mills quake in the 1990s in Oregon. They got shaken pretty hard in Portland by the Nisqually Quake, but the shelving held!

I'm sure that brick would fall in a solid enough earthquake but I don't think that building will fall.  They don't require businesses or private homes to retrofit for earthquakes but I have talked everyone into doing it that I know who owns a house because it only makes sense and much of it is pretty inexpensive to do also. I also keep hand tools in my room with me just in case the building falls anyway and I have to dig my own way out, plus then I know right where that stuff is in case I need to dig my neighbors out. Obviously, I also have food, water, good shoes, flashlights (including multiple solar ones) because that's the basic stuff I've had available everywhere I've lived for decades of living in Southern California. Then there are more extensive survival things both in the garage at the edge of it and in a separate shed. If even a relatively poor person can do all of this, so can all of you. I remember the 1989 World Series Earthquake because I was trying to watch the World Series and I realized that the announcer had said there was an earthquake right before it cut out so I was waiting to see when I'd feel it but I never did. That was the first earthquake I heard about but did not feel so I wonder if it would be the same with a 9 since that would be even further to the north, but also much bigger.
